records.sourceFile: Cross-validation of the safe supplement screener (S3) predicting consistent third-party-tested nutritional supplement use in NCAA Division I athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Schott KD, Bhalla A, Armstrong E, Seltzer RGN, Wardenaar FC. Cross-validation of the safe supplement screener (S3) predicting consistent third-party-tested nutritional supplement use in NCAA Division I athletes. Front Nutr. 2025;11:1519544.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey of NCAA Division I athletes tested whether an earlier algorithm-based screener (S3) predicts consistent use of third-party-tested (TPT) supplements. The original algorithm was confirmed to separate consistent from inconsistent users, with a 60% cut-off, but with modest accuracy. A new exploratory model identified TPT logo recognition and having a name, image, likeness deal as additional associated variables.
paper.tldr: The S3 screener flags most athletes who do not consistently use third-party-tested supplements, but it also flags many who do, so it should be used as a conversation starter rather than a verdict. Two new questions, logo recognition and NIL deal status, may be worth adding, but they need further validation.
paper.methods: A web-based questionnaire was completed by 725 athletes from eight Pac-12 athletic departments between September 2023 and January 2024. The authors applied the existing S3 algorithm to 662 supplement users, computed sensitivity, specificity and AUC at a 60% risk cut-off, and ran stepwise logistic regression to explore additional predictors.
paper.findings: The original S3 algorithm showed a significant association with TPT use (chi-square 15.95, p < 0.001) with AUC 0.67, sensitivity 68% and specificity 51% at the 60% cut-off. The exploratory model identified TPT logo recognition and NIL deal status, and showed AUC 0.73, sensitivity 85% and specificity 40% at its cut-off (Table 6).
paper.limitations: The abstract reports sensitivity as 51% and specificity as 68%, which is the reverse of Table 4 (sensitivity 68%, specificity 51%); this record uses the table values. The Discussion says the new model had lower sensitivity and higher specificity, but Table 6 shows the opposite (sensitivity 85%, specificity 40%). The new predictors were selected and tested on the same data, the sample is self-reported from one conference, and the lead screener developer disclosed an award linked to the S3.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports dietitians and athletic trainers can use the S3 questions to ask athletes about TPT use, familiarity with WADA-banned substances and where they buy supplements. A high screener score should prompt a conversation about tested products, not a conclusion that an athlete is unsafe, because many consistent users also scored high.
paper.athleteDev: This paper addresses supplement safety behaviour, not performance outcomes. It can inform how performance staff discuss tested supplement choices with athletes, but it does not show that any supplement improves performance.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The study surveyed healthy collegiate athletes about supplement use and did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Characterizing hydration practices in healthy young recreationally active adults - Is there utility in first morning urine sampling.pdf

paper.citation: Muñoz CX, Bergeron MF. Characterizing hydration practices in healthy young recreationally active adults: is there utility in first morning urine sampling? Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2023. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: This study tested whether a single first morning urine (FMU) sample reflects hydration practices over the previous 24 hours and 5 days in 67 healthy young adults. FMU osmolality had the best diagnostic accuracy, FMU colour had little utility, and the authors propose FMU as a low-cost way to screen for underhydration.
paper.tldr: A first morning urine osmolality of about 710 mOsm/kg or higher flagged young adults whose previous day's urine was concentrated (above 500 mOsm/kg), with accuracy above 80%. Urine colour on waking was not a useful substitute, and the cut-offs have not been tested in athletes.
paper.methods: Over 5 consecutive days, 67 participants (38 women, 29 men) kept 24-hour diet logs for total water intake, collected all urine for osmolality, specific gravity and colour, and gave morning blood for plasma osmolality and copeptin; FMU was collected on the final morning only. Correlations and ROC analysis tested FMU against published underhydration thresholds (water intake below 30 ml/kg, urine osmolality above 500 and 800 mOsm/kg, specific gravity above 1.017, copeptin above 6.93 pmol/L), with an AUC of 0.80 or more counted as useful.
paper.findings: FMU osmolality and specific gravity correlated significantly with all variables except 5-day plasma osmolality, at weak to moderate strength (r up to 0.78), while FMU colour correlated only with other colour measures and water intake in grams. FMU osmolality of 710 mOsm/kg or more detected a previous 24-hour urine osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg with AUC, sensitivity and specificity above 80% (positive likelihood ratio 5.9), but it did not meet the 0.80 AUC criterion for low water intake (AUC 0.77 to 0.79) or raised copeptin (AUC 0.67 to 0.73). FMU specific gravity met the criterion for 5-day urine osmolality, and the authors suggest an FMU specific gravity criterion of 1.021.
paper.limitations: Participants were not athletes, exercised under 2.5 hours a week (although 13 exceeded this), and refrained from exercise for 12 hours before visits, so results may not transfer to athletes with daily sweat losses. FMU was collected only once, water intake relied on self-reported logs, and thresholds were derived and tested in the same sample. Several AUC, sensitivity and specificity values appear only in figures that are not readable in the extracted text.
paper.practicalImplications: Where 24-hour urine collection is impractical, FMU osmolality is a candidate low-cost screen for habitually concentrated urine, with about 710 mOsm/kg as this study's criterion for a previous-day urine osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg. FMU colour should not be relied on alone. Thresholds for athletes after training or heat exposure are not established by this study.
paper.athleteDev: The authors frame FMU as a way to detect underhydration before training or competition, but they did not study athletes or measure performance. It cannot show that acting on an FMU result improves performance.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Participants were healthy young adults and the study did not assess injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Role of sports psychology and sports nutrition in return to play from musculoskeletal injuries in professional soccer an interdisciplinary approach.pdf

paper.citation: Rollo I, Carter JM, Close GL, Yangüas J, Gomez-Diaz A, Medina Leal D, et al. Role of sports psychology and sports nutrition in return to play from musculoskeletal injuries in professional soccer: an interdisciplinary approach. Eur J Sport Sci. 2020.
paper.abstract: Musculoskeletal injuries are common in professional soccer, and return to play depends mainly on medical staff. This paper proposes how sports psychology and sports nutrition can be integrated into a physician-led, phased return-to-play framework covering the acute injury and functional recovery phases.
paper.tldr: Psychology and nutrition support can be built into the medical return-to-play milestones for injured soccer players, covering pain and distress, eating behaviour, motivation and body composition. The evidence for whether this improves outcomes over medical care alone is not yet available.
paper.methods: This is a narrative review and framework paper written by authors from sports nutrition, sports psychology, sports medicine and performance backgrounds. It draws on consensus statements, experimental and applied studies, and the authors' practical experience at professional clubs, and organises the content by the acute injury and functional recovery phases.
paper.findings: The authors propose psychological tools such as imagery, goal setting and education for the acute phase, and nutrition plans to maintain energy and lean mass, with example protein, fish oil, creatine, vitamin D and collagen strategies drawn from immobilisation and laboratory studies. They suggest that interdisciplinary meetings at each milestone, body composition tracking and performance monitoring can support return to play. They state that the benefit of this approach over single-discipline care has not been established.
paper.limitations: No original data are presented, and the paper does not report a systematic search or evidence grading. The authors state that long-term effects on performance, well-being and re-injury are not yet established, and the milestone timelines in Figure 1 are estimates from FC Barcelona data and clinical experience. Two authors are employees of the Gatorade Sports Science Institute, a division of PepsiCo, which is disclosed.
paper.practicalImplications: Team physicians, physiotherapists, sports dietitians and sport psychologists can agree shared milestones early in an injury, with a single clinician leading the plan. Nutrition and psychological education can give injured players a sense of control while the medical plan runs. Specific supplement doses in the paper should be checked against current evidence and product testing before use.
paper.athleteDev: Not a performance paper. It suggests that performance staff can keep injured players engaged through structured nutrition and psychological support, and continue monitoring nutrition after a player returns to full training, but it does not measure performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: This paper is directly about return to play. It can inform how psychological and nutritional support are coordinated with medical milestones, but it cannot establish the timing of return, show that these supports shorten recovery, or set a clearance criterion for a player.

records.sourceFile: Nutrition for the prevention and treatment of injuries in track and field athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Close GL, Sale C, Baar K, Bermon S. Nutrition for the prevention and treatment of injuries in track and field athletes. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(2):189-197.
paper.abstract: Injuries are common in athletics, with skeletal muscle injuries making up over 40% of cases. This review examines nutrition strategies, including protein, energy availability, vitamin D, calcium, omega-3 fats, creatine, vitamin C, copper and gelatin or collagen, for reducing injury risk and aiding recovery in muscle, bone, tendon and ligament.
paper.tldr: Avoiding low energy availability and dietary deficiencies is the best-supported nutrition step for reducing bone injury risk in track and field athletes. For muscle, tendon and ligament injuries, the evidence for specific supplements is limited and mostly indirect.
paper.methods: This is a scholarly narrative review by four authors with sport nutrition, sports medicine and athletics federation backgrounds. The authors summarise epidemiology from international championship surveillance and review nutrition studies in muscle damage models, bone health, tendon loading and animal and small human studies. The text does not describe a systematic search.
paper.findings: About 81 injuries per 1,000 athletes were recorded at a World Championship, and skeletal muscle injuries made up 40.9% of injuries. The review links low energy availability to reduced bone formation, and cites evidence that very low energy availability of about 10 kcal per kg lean mass also increases bone resorption. For muscle, a systematic review found no measurable effect of acute protein on exercise-induced muscle damage, but the authors suggest injured limbs may benefit from higher protein intake, and the gelatin study they cite (15 g versus 5 g) doubled collagen synthesis in a single placebo-controlled crossover study.
paper.limitations: The authors state there are no placebo-controlled randomised trials of nutrition after a true muscle injury in elite athletes. Much of the muscle evidence is from exercise-induced damage models, and the bone and tendon evidence is partly extrapolated from general bone health, military recruits and animal studies. Some gelatin and ligament results are unpublished or come from engineered ligaments in vitro.
paper.practicalImplications: Sports dietitians can check that athletes are not chronically low in energy availability, which the review identifies as a major bone injury risk, and can plan calorie cycling around competition. During an injury, the review supports keeping protein high and avoiding large energy cuts, with supplements such as vitamin D used when a deficiency is confirmed and tested for contamination.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who plan training and competition fuelling. The review links low energy availability and nutrient gaps to bone injury risk, but it does not show that any nutrition strategy improves sprint, jump or throw performance.
paper.rtp: Partly relevant to return to sport. The review offers guidance on protein, energy and micronutrient intake during recovery from muscle, bone, tendon and ligament injury, but the authors state that the evidence for speeding recovery is indirect and cannot set a return-to-sport timeline or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Hydration Marker Diagnostic   Accuracy to Identify Mild Intracellular and Extracellular Dehydration.pdf

paper.citation: Owen JA, Fortes MB, Ur Rahman S, Jibani M, Walsh NP, Oliver SJ. Hydration marker diagnostic accuracy to identify mild intracellular and extracellular dehydration. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2019;29(6):604-611.
paper.abstract: In 15 young healthy men, the diagnostic accuracy of 15 hydration markers was tested after euhydration, mild intracellular dehydration from exercise and fluid restriction, and mild extracellular dehydration from diuretic use. Thirst on a 0-9 scale and urine osmolality identified both dehydration types, and a thirst score of 4 or more was the only threshold that worked for both.
paper.tldr: A simple 0-9 thirst rating, with a cut-off of 4 or more, detected about 2% body mass loss in young men with reasonable accuracy in both exercise-type and diuretic-type dehydration. It is a practical screen, but it needs testing in women, older adults and other conditions before wider use.
paper.methods: Fifteen healthy men completed three randomised 48-hour trials: euhydration, intracellular dehydration (exercise and water restriction to 2 ml per kg per day), and extracellular dehydration (furosemide with a 4-hour diuresis). Fifteen hydration markers were measured, including thirst, urine, saliva, heart rate variability, postural changes and plasma osmolality. Accuracy was assessed with ROC-AUC and Youden-derived thresholds, with body mass change as the reference.
paper.findings: Body mass fell by 1.9% after intracellular dehydration and 2.0% after extracellular dehydration. Thirst 0-9 had ROC-AUC 0.97 for intracellular and 0.78 for extracellular dehydration, and urine osmolality had 0.99 and 0.81 (Table 3), with a thirst threshold of 4 or more giving sensitivity 99% and specificity 87% for intracellular, and 71% and 87% for extracellular dehydration (Table 4). Tear osmolality, supine blood pressure and supine heart rate did not discriminate either type.
paper.limitations: The abstract reports sensitivity of 100% for the thirst threshold, but Table 4 shows 99% for intracellular dehydration. The sample was 15 young men only, dehydration was induced in a controlled laboratory, and thresholds were not tested on separate participants. The extracellular dehydration accuracy for thirst (ROC-AUC 0.78, lower confidence bound 0.59) is moderate, and the authors note that thirst may differ in women, older adults and people taking medications.
paper.practicalImplications: Practitioners working with young men in similar conditions can ask for a 0-9 thirst rating, with 4 or more suggesting mild dehydration needing fluid intake, as the authors recommend thirst as the initial screen. Urine osmolality also discriminated both types, but its thresholds differed by dehydration type (above 595 mOsm/kg for intracellular, above 341 mOsm/kg for extracellular), and urine specific gravity and colour identified only intracellular dehydration. Do not apply the thirst threshold to women, older athletes or heat exposure without further validation.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff because the paper frames mild dehydration as the level at which performance is affected, and it offers a low-cost fluid check. The study did not measure any performance outcome, so it cannot show that correcting the thirst-flagged deficit improves performance.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The participants were healthy men without injury, and the study did not assess rehabilitation, injury or recovery outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Coingestion of carbohydrate and protein on muscle glycogen synthesis after exercise - A meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Margolis LM, Allen JT, Hatch-McChesney A, Pasiakos SM. Coingestion of carbohydrate and protein on muscle glycogen synthesis after exercise: a meta-analysis. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(2):384-393.
paper.abstract: This meta-analysis of 20 crossover studies compared carbohydrate-plus-protein with carbohydrate alone for muscle glycogen replenishment after exercise. Overall, the combined drink did not significantly increase glycogen synthesis, but it did when it provided more total energy than carbohydrate alone.
paper.tldr: Adding protein to a carbohydrate recovery drink improved muscle glycogen replenishment only when it added energy on top of the carbohydrate. When total energy was matched, protein did not add a measurable benefit to glycogen synthesis.
paper.methods: Crossover trials comparing carbohydrate-plus-protein with carbohydrate alone for post-exercise glycogen synthesis were identified from PubMed and the Cochrane Library, with a PRISMA-based search. Twenty studies with 23 intervention groups were pooled using Hedges' g and random effects. Subgroup analyses split studies by isocaloric versus non-isocaloric designs and by high versus low relative carbohydrate intake (median 0.8 g per kg per hour).
paper.findings: The overall effect was 0.13 (95% CI -0.04 to 0.29), not significant. Non-isocaloric comparisons showed a positive effect of 0.26 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.49), while isocaloric comparisons showed -0.05 (95% CI -0.23 to 0.13). In the isocaloric studies, carbohydrate-plus-protein gave similar glycogen synthesis to carbohydrate alone despite about 30% less carbohydrate (mean 0.63 vs 0.86 g per kg per hour, plus 0.22 g per kg per hour of protein, Table 3).
paper.limitations: The overall heterogeneity was substantial (I2 = 71%), and publication bias was detected (P = 0.03), driven by positive studies in the non-isocaloric group. The sample was 158 men and 18 women in laboratory studies, and a correlation of 0.80 was imputed for all studies. The abstract reports the high-carbohydrate subgroup CI as -0.11 to 0.22, but the Results text gives -0.11 to 0.25.
paper.practicalImplications: Adding protein on top of a fixed carbohydrate dose increased glycogen synthesis in the pooled non-isocaloric studies, while replacing part of the carbohydrate with protein at equal energy gave similar glycogen synthesis to carbohydrate alone. The authors suggest about 0.9 g per kg per hour of carbohydrate plus 0.3 g per kg per hour of protein as an energy-matched alternative to 1.2 g per kg per hour of carbohydrate, which also supports muscle protein synthesis, but this specific split was not tested as a subgroup.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who plan fuelling between sessions, especially for athletes with two sessions a day. The study measures glycogen synthesis, not performance, and the authors note that one study reported a performance increase while systematic reviews found no overall performance benefit.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The studies used healthy trained or untrained adults in laboratory exercise, not injured athletes, and did not assess rehabilitation, tissue healing or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Efectiveness of Education Interventions Designed to Improve Nutrition Knowledge in Athletes- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Tam R, Beck KL, Manore MM, Gifford J, Flood VM, O'Connor H. Effectiveness of education interventions designed to improve nutrition knowledge in athletes: a systematic review. Sports Med. 2019.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 32 studies tested nutrition education interventions aimed at improving nutrition knowledge in athletes. Most interventions reported significant knowledge gains, but the wide range of knowledge tools and the predominance of face-to-face delivery prevented identification of the most effective method or dose.
paper.tldr: Nutrition education programmes for athletes usually raise nutrition knowledge scores, but the included studies are short and mostly used tools with limited validation. The review cannot say which teaching method or how much contact time works best.
paper.methods: Six databases were searched up to June 2019, with hand searching of reference lists, for original human research in athletes of any level that used a scored knowledge test before and after an education intervention. Study quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist, and Hedges' g effect sizes were calculated. A meta-analysis was not conducted because of variation in tools and interventions.
paper.findings: Thirteen RCTs (weighted mean change +19.2% for intervention groups, ES 2.9, versus +2.2% for controls) and 19 single-arm studies (+12.7%, ES 0.88) reported knowledge change, with 30 of 35 interventions (85.7%) showing significant gains. Average quality was 17 of 28 for RCTs and 11.7 of 22 for single-arm studies. Most interventions were face-to-face and under 5 hours of total contact time.
paper.limitations: The authors state that only 15.6% of studies used well-validated knowledge tools, and most were author-designed or modified. Only two studies assessed knowledge retention, no meta-analysis was performed, and individual effect sizes varied widely (one RCT reported 17.1), so the 1.72 average is a descriptive figure rather than a pooled estimate. Searching and screening were done by one author, and no RCT blinded participants, facilitators or outcome assessment.
paper.practicalImplications: Short group education programmes can produce measurable knowledge gains in athletes. The authors recommend establishing the validity and reliability of the knowledge test before running a programme, and handouts alone produced smaller gains than presentations or cooking classes in the two studies that compared them. Technology-based delivery had lower attrition in the four studies that used it, so it may be worth piloting, but it is not yet shown to be superior.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who run nutrition education as part of athlete development. The review shows knowledge gains, but it does not measure dietary behaviour, body composition or performance, so it cannot show that education improves performance.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The review did not examine injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Interaction Between Caffeine and Creatine When Used as Concurrent Ergogenic Supplements_- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Elosegui S, López-Seoane J, Martínez-Ferrán M, Pareja-Galeano H. Interaction between caffeine and creatine when used as concurrent ergogenic supplements: a systematic review. Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab. 2022. Ahead of print.
paper.abstract: This systematic review of 10 placebo-controlled trials examined whether caffeine and creatine interact when taken together to enhance exercise performance, and what doses allow their combined use. Acute caffeine after creatine loading did not impair the benefit, while chronic combined use gave mixed results across studies.
paper.tldr: Taking caffeine on the day of a session after a creatine loading phase did not appear to reduce creatine's benefits. Daily caffeine during creatine loading gave conflicting results, and the review suggests it could interfere.
paper.methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, MEDLINE, CINAHL and SPORTDiscus up to November 2021 followed PRISMA. Included studies were randomised, placebo-controlled trials in healthy adults that gave creatine and caffeine together and measured performance. Risk of bias was rated with the Cochrane tool.
paper.findings: Three studies found that creatine loading before an acute caffeine dose did not interfere with caffeine's effect. For chronic use, one study reported synergy, two reported that caffeine interfered with creatine's effect on muscle relaxation time or torque, and three showed no interaction. The authors suggest that creatine loading does not seem to affect acute caffeine effects, but chronic caffeine during creatine loading could interfere with creatine's benefit.
paper.limitations: The authors describe small sample sizes, few randomised and blinded trials, heterogeneous supplementation protocols and exercise tests, and gastrointestinal discomfort reported in some trials. The included trials were mostly male, aged 18 to 25, and conducted in laboratories.
paper.practicalImplications: In the three trials that gave 5 to 6 mg per kg of caffeine about an hour before exercise after a creatine loading phase, caffeine's ergogenic effects were preserved. Daily caffeine during creatine loading is the scenario with conflicting results, including blunted dynamic torque and relaxation-time benefits, so staff may prefer to avoid it until better evidence is available. Gastrointestinal tolerance should be monitored when both are used.
paper.athleteDev: Relevant to performance staff who advise athletes on combined supplements. The review reports performance outcomes such as time to exhaustion, sprint power and torque, but the evidence is small and mixed, so it cannot promise a performance gain from combining the two.
paper.rtp: Cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. The review excluded injured or ill participants and did not assess rehabilitation, tissue healing or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Supplementation of probiotics and   its effects on physically active individuals and athletes - Systematic   review.pdf

paper.citation: Möller GB, Goulart MJVC, Nicoletto BB, Alves FD, Schneider CD. Supplementation of Probiotics and Its Effects on Physically Active Individuals and Athletes: Systematic Review. International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism. 2019;29(5):481-492.
paper.abstract: This systematic review pooled findings from 24 controlled trials of probiotic supplementation in healthy adults who exercise, including athletes and physically active people. The trials included 1,680 participants, 67.5% of them male, with a mean age of 30.9 years. Five databases were searched, and study quality was rated with GRADE.
paper.tldr: Probiotics reduced respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms in some trials of physically active people, but results were inconsistent. The review found weak evidence that probiotics improve exercise performance.
paper.methods: A PRISMA-based systematic review (registered as CRD42017070151) searched MEDLINE, Embase, SciELO, Scopus and Lilacs. Two reviewers screened studies and extracted data independently, and GRADE was used to rate evidence quality. Eligible studies were controlled trials of probiotics in healthy adults who exercised, with no pooled statistical analysis.
paper.findings: The authors report that five trials showed fewer respiratory symptoms or shorter or milder illness with probiotics (their list cites six), and two more reported fewer respiratory episodes, while three found no respiratory effect. Most trials found no effect on immune markers, and inflammatory and gut permeability results were mixed. Performance was assessed in seven studies, and the authors judged that evidence weak and inconclusive.
paper.limitations: The trials were small and varied in strain, dose, duration, outcomes and population, which makes the results hard to compare. No meta-analysis was done, and two studies were excluded because their authors could not be contacted. The abstract and discussion state that probiotics improved immunologic markers, but the results report that most studies found no immune effect; the results are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Probiotics may help reduce some respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms in physically active people, but the benefit was not consistent across trials. Any product should match the strain and dose that were tested. This review does not support claims of better performance or immune protection for all athletes.
paper.athleteDev: This review does not support using probiotics as a performance aid, because the performance evidence was weak and mixed. Any use should be framed as an illness-prevention option to discuss with the medical staff.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It includes no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: The paradoxical effect of creatine monohydrate on muscle damage markers - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Doma K, Ramachandran AK, Boullosa D, Connor J. The Paradoxical Effect of Creatine Monohydrate on Muscle Damage Markers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 23 placebo-controlled trials of creatine monohydrate (CrM) in healthy adults exposed to muscle-damaging exercise. Outcomes were indirect damage markers, inflammation, oxidative stress, muscle soreness and muscle force at 24-36 h and 48-90 h, and the trials were split into single-bout (acute) and multi-week training (chronic) responses.
paper.tldr: Creatine was linked to lower muscle damage markers 2 to 4 days after a single hard session, but after several weeks of training the same markers were higher with creatine at 24 h. Creatine did not clearly improve recovery of muscle force or soreness.
paper.methods: A PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42020207421) searched PubMed, Scopus, SPORTDiscus, CINAHL and Web of Science in August 2021. Two reviewers screened studies, one author rated quality with a modified PEDro scale, and random-effects meta-analyses of standardised mean differences were run with Egger's test where at least ten studies were available.
paper.findings: After a single bout, damage markers were lower with CrM at 48-90 h (SMD -1.09, p = 0.03) but not at 24-36 h, and oxidative stress was lower at 24-36 h (SMD -1.37, p < 0.001); inflammation showed large but non-significant reductions. After training, damage markers were higher with CrM at 24 h (SMD 0.95, p = 0.04), and the 48 h difference was large but not significant (p = 0.06). Muscle force and soreness differences were not significant.
paper.limitations: Training status ranged from sedentary and older adults to trained athletes, and only about 10% of participants were female. Protocols, doses, damage markers and follow-up times varied with high heterogeneity, and over 70% of studies did not assess creatine bioavailability. The abstract states that oxidative stress differences were not significant, but the results report a significant difference at 24-36 h (p < 0.001); the results values are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: Creatine around a single strenuous session was linked to lower damage markers 2 to 4 days later, but not at 24 h and not on every marker. Staff should not expect creatine to speed recovery of muscle force or soreness on this evidence. During long creatine-supported training blocks, damage markers may read higher at 24 h, so interpret creatine kinase values with supplement use in mind.
paper.athleteDev: The review does not show that creatine improves performance or muscle force recovery, so it should not be promoted as a recovery aid on this evidence. Any change in training load because of creatine should be guided by monitored soreness and damage, not assumed benefit.
paper.rtp: This review cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It studied healthy adults after exercise-induced muscle damage, with no injured athletes and no return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: Dietary inorganic nitrate as an ergogenic aid - An expert consensus derived via the modified Delphi technique.pdf

paper.citation: Shannon OM, Allen JD, Bescos R, Burke L, Clifford T, Easton C, et al. Dietary Inorganic Nitrate as an Ergogenic Aid: An Expert Consensus Derived via the Modified Delphi Technique. Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: A 12-member expert panel used a modified Delphi technique over three rounds to vote on 222 statements about dietary inorganic nitrate as an ergogenic aid. Statements covered activity type, population, supplementation strategy, physiological effects, safety and toxicity, quality of evidence, and the ethos of Olympic sport. Consensus required more than 80% agreement.
paper.tldr: An expert panel agreed on some practical points for dietary nitrate, including doses, timing before exercise, and benefit mainly at low to moderate aerobic fitness. Most questions were judged to have insufficient evidence.
paper.methods: Twelve experts (PhD-qualified, with publications or applied experience) completed three voting rounds on 222 statements: two anonymous questionnaire rounds and one videoconference discussion. Consensus was defined a priori as more than 80% agreement, and statements with more than 80% insufficient-evidence votes were removed from further voting.
paper.findings: Thirty-nine statements (17.6%) reached consensus: 20 yes and 19 no. Acute doses of 8-16 mmol and chronic doses of 4-16 mmol/day were judged ergogenic, taken 2-4 h before exercise, with beetroot juice and nitrate salts supported as forms. Benefit was agreed for low aerobic fitness (VO2peak below 45 ml/kg/min) and for chronic use at moderate fitness (below 60 ml/kg/min), and acute doses up to about 16 mmol were judged safe. The panel agreed the 3.7 mg/kg/day ADI is not appropriate, and no consensus was reached on sex or age effects.
paper.limitations: Expert opinion from 12 panelists is subjective and may not represent all researchers. The panel had less experience with clinical populations, and the clinical statements were broad. Sex, age and sport-specific effects were largely left as insufficient evidence. Nine of the 16 listed authors reported receiving discounted or free beetroot juice for research, one received free nitrate gels, and several reported industry-linked funding or consultancy.
paper.practicalImplications: For athletes with low to moderate aerobic fitness, the consensus supports considering nitrate at 8-16 mmol before a single session or 4-16 mmol/day over several days, with the dose taken 2-4 h before exercise. The panel agreed beetroot juice and nitrate salts are ergogenic, but the authors advise vegetable-derived sources such as beetroot juice for safety. The authors judge effects diminished above about 60 ml/kg/min VO2peak, and most other questions, including specific sports, sex and age, remain unsettled.
paper.athleteDev: Dietary nitrate is most likely to help athletes with low to moderate aerobic fitness. The panel reached no consensus that it helps highly trained athletes, and the authors conclude effects appear diminished above about 60 ml/kg/min VO2peak. Performance changes should be checked against an individual baseline, since the panel found insufficient evidence for most sport-specific effects.
paper.rtp: This consensus cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. Its statements about clinical populations were largely judged insufficient or without consensus, and it does not address injured athletes.
